newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Malaise strikes gold while zinc zips higher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaise strikes gold while zinc zips higher.

text.p: Malaise continued to strike an anaemic gold market on Friday as the precious metal slumped to its most depressed level in nearly 4-1/4 years.

The dollar's continued strength coupled with further short selling by industry dealers contributed to its demise, although many now suggest gold could finally be hitting rock bottom, if only because things have been so bad they seem unlikely to get worse.
"When a market looks as bad as this it is a sure sign the price is at the bottom," one dealer said.
Bullion was fixed at $336.55 per ounce in the afternoon -- its lowest level since April 1, 1993. It then struggled to maintain that level in late London trade.

Others argued that gold could continue losing its fading glint because inflation remained firmly under control in most major economies and there appeared little chance of a financial crisis reactivating its safe haven status.

Elsewhere in the commodity markets, base metals put in a volatile day as zinc hit fresh seven year highs while nickel prices sank below $7,000 a tonne amid signs that a strike at the largest producer in the West could soon be ending.

Zinc, used to galvanise steel and alloyed with copper to make brass, has been a darling of speculators seeking to capitalise on a healthy global economy by betting on a base metal with low producer and consumer stocks.
It finished the day in London at $1,428 a tonne after peaking at $1,430.

Union negotiators at Canada's Inco Ltd announced they have endorsed a contract deal to end a four-week strike at the company's Sudbury, Ontario plant. But the deal must still be approved by strikers in a vote to be held on Saturday.
The division had been expected to produce 230 million pounds of nickel, which is mostly used to manufacture stainless steel, and 200 million pounds of copper this year.
The base metal hit a 6-1/2 month low of $6,930 per tonne in late afternoon trade on the London Metal Exchange versus $7,070 on Thursday.

Crude oil was one of the day's few strong performers when it made a push higher in the wake of short-term supply tightness in the Atlantic basin and lingering worries about the absence of Iraqi barrels from the market.

The oil market also faced a positive technical picture which drove some financial funds to cover their short positions, traders said, cautioning they would likely resume a bearish outlook early next month.
Despite the day's gains many dealers expected prices to begin falling again soon bcause of a likely resumption of Iraqi exports next month and excess OPEC output.
Coffee notched up a mixed performance by dipping nearly one percent in London on follow-through selling after New York's sharp overnight fall.
More mild weather in Brazil's coffee-growing areas forecast for the next five days continued to overhang the market.

"The main danger now is that it is so warm that the predicted rains could actually lead to flowerings three months ahead of normal," broker GNI said. "It looks like a one-way street for coffee now. It's very difficult to be bullish," said one trader.

Cocoa prices firmed slightly in London and appeared to have entered a consolidation period after their sharp rally of the last two weeks. Aggressive fund and speculative buying fuelled the run-up, aided by manufacturers covering their outstanding short positions.
